speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, it seeks to streamline Court procedures to enhance efficiency, introduce flexibility in order to meet shifting trends and also accommodate the needs of individual cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, it empowers the Courts to better manage vexatious or tardy conduct in proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the main, the amendments will allow the Courts to operate more effectively and efficiently, without compromising access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that judicial resources are better allocated, and results in time and cost savings for litigants and lawyers alike.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now take the House through the key features of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Technology has significantly changed the way we live and conduct our affairs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With the advancement of technology, we are able to accomplish tasks in a much faster and efficient manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similarly, if used meaningfully, technology has the ability to also make a positive impact on the way our Courts function.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Previously, apart from the provision of evidence by witnesses in civil proceedings, the law did not provide for the general conduct of hearings through electronic means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: With this amendment, legal proceedings which do not require the physical presence of parties or their lawyers in Court can be conducted quickly and more efficiently via electronic means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This enhances the Court process and saves time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also grants the Courts various powers so that they can swiftly dispose cases in the most appropriate manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, clause 6 of the Bill expands the range of cases that can be decided based on written submissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, the Court of Appeal may decide any application for leave to appeal based on written submissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendment only empowers the Court of Appeal to decide any application to it without hearing oral arguments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, an application in contrast to substantive appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The scope of this amendment does not extend to cover other substantive appeals, except for those which emanate from the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) and, even then, in situations where parties agree.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Where the Court of Appeal is of the view that even with this power, oral arguments are necessary, it will continue to retain the power to, and will, in fact, hear such oral arguments before deciding the application or appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, where the Court lacks jurisdiction to hear and determine the appeal or application; or second, where there is no merit in the appeal or application because the issue has been decided by the Court of Appeal in an earlier matter in which the appellant or applicant was involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This clause allows unmeritorious appeals or applications to be dismissed without expending unnecessary judicial time and resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, safeguards are put in place to ensure that the interests of the appellant or applicant are adequately protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In this regard, before a Court can summarily dismiss an appeal or application, it must give the appellant or applicant a reasonable opportunity to show cause as to why the appeal or application should not be dismissed and consider the representations of the appellant or applicant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, we are also proposing amendments in relation to the admission of further evidence on appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, further evidence can be admitted, on appeal, without leave of Court: one, in relation to interlocutory applications; and two, where matters occurred subsequent to the date of the earlier decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In line with efficient judicial administration, parties should be encouraged to present all relevant evidence at the first instance hearing so that cases can be disposed fairly, efficiently and also comprehensively based on available evidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This means that parties who seek to admit further evidence on interlocutory applications will now require leave of Court in order to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will ensure that only meritorious applications to adduce further evidence will be allowed to proceed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the same vein, clause 8 introduces a new requirement for leave of Court to make an application to discharge or vary incidental directions or orders made by the Court under section 36 of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in respect of directions or orders which are ancillary to the main appeal and are unlikely to touch on the substantive merits of the case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The requirement for leave of Court ensures that Court resources would be directed appropriately to deal only with meritorious applications to discharge or vary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In deciding whether to grant leave or not for a party to vary or discharge a direction or order under section 36, the Court of Appeal will consider if such directions and orders are, in fact, ancillary to the appeal, or whether they go towards the merits of the appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Leave would be granted where it would be in the interest of justice to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, the Bill also seeks to introduce flexibility and efficiency in the Court process to allow for cases to be heard expeditiously and also have regard to the various shifting trends that may rise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In this regard, clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill introduce amendments to allow for matters relating to, firstly, the coram of the Court of Appeal, and secondly, as to which matters are non-appealable or only appealable with leave to the Court of Appeal, to be moved from the primary Act into the Fourth to Sixth Schedules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As to the coram of the Court of Appeal, section 30(1) of the Act states that the civil jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal shall be exercised by three or any greater uneven number of Judges of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Section 30(2) sets out the types of matters which can be determined by a Court of Appeal consisting of two Judges of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill will seek to introduce a new Sixth Schedule which would set out the number of judges that would be required to exercise the civil jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal for different matters, as specified in that Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Members can be assured that when the matters are moved into the Sixth Schedule, they will continue to reflect the current position that is based on section 30.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As regards appeals on certain matters, the current section 34(1) and the Fourth Schedule set out the matters which are non-appealable to the Court of Appeal, while section 34(2) and the Fifth Schedule set out the matters which are appealable only with leave to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: By clause 5 of the Bill, matters which are non-appealable will now be set out in the Fourth Schedule, and matters which are appealable only with leave will be set out in the Fifth Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, part of the amendments seeks to consolidate all the items into one Schedule rather than have them appear in parts of the Bill and in the existing Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The only exception to this would be section 34(2)(a), which sets out the jurisdictional monetary limit and threshold.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This, because it deals with the question of jurisdictional monetary limit, will remain in the primary Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These amendments allow for a quicker revision of each of the above categories as amendments of the primary legislation would require more time to effect rather than the amendment of the Schedule itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Placing these matters in the Schedules, therefore, allows more flexibility and speed as they can be amended by the Minister, in consultation with the Chief Justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Schedules can be revised swiftly to ensure that an efficient allocation of judicial resources can be balanced against the volume of appeals, so that the Court of Appeal can handle deserving cases expeditiously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As to the second point I raised earlier, clause 14 seeks to clarify that under section 80(2)(h), the Rules Committee is empowered to make rules relating to the manner in which factual, expert or opinion evidence is to be presented in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I turn now to the next basket of amendments that deal with vexatious proceedings and tardy conduct in the legal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Vexatious litigation is a drain on our Court resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They draw away precious Court time from dealing with meritorious applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Court of Appeal has had the opportunity to define vexatious proceedings in recent case law, and these amendments do not seek to change that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Broadly, vexatious proceedings are those which are groundless and without merit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They may be initiated with the purpose of annoying or embarrassing the other party, and not for the purpose of having the Court decide on the issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Apart from wasting judicial resources, vexatious conduct, especially when instituted habitually and persistently, causes distress and annoyance to other parties to the proceedings as they are subject to a litany of baseless lawsuits and applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, section 74 of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act provides the only recourse against such vexatious litigants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If a party has habitually and persistently and without any reasonable grounds instituted vexatious legal proceedings in any Court, it is the Attorney-General who has to make an application to the Court to restrain such conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And upon the making of such a successful application, the High Court may order that: a) either no legal proceedings be instituted by that party without the leave of Court, and/or b) any legal proceedings instituted by that party in any Court before the making of the order shall not be continued by him without leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This current approach is limited in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the Court and the affected party have no power to act on their own to apply under section 74 regardless of the degree of vexatious conduct, the impact it may have had on the affected party, as the application must be made by the Attorney-General.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, section 74 carries with it severe consequences and may not be proportionate to or properly calibrated to meet the mischief in question in all cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The three different types of orders are as follows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This order may be made against a party who has made two or more applications that are totally without merit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The party will be restrained from making further applications in the particular proceedings in which the order is made, without leave of Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This order may be made against a party who has persistently commenced actions or made applications that are totally without merit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such an order may be made against a party who has persisted in commencing action or making applications that are totally without merit, and in circumstances where an extended civil restraint order would not be sufficient or appropriate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The party will be restrained from commencing any action or making any application in any Court specified in the order, without leave of Court for a period not exceeding two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This gradated approach gives more nuance in managing vexatious litigants, taking into account the specific facts of each case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Court will also be empowered to stay the vexatious proceedings and order that no further documents be filed by a party if the filing of documents would be vexatious or otherwise for an improper purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Before an order is made against a party, that party will be given an opportunity to be heard by the Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In relation to proceedings before a lower Court, a party or the Attorney-General may make an application to the High Court for one of the abovementioned orders, so to the extent that this may appear in the district Courts or the magistrate's Courts, an application is made to the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This power ensures that the High Court can also make the necessary orders to address vexatious proceedings occurring before a lower Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is more appropriate for the High Court to make such orders, instead of the lower Court, because the impact of such orders is potentially far-reaching and restrains a party’s ability to conduct legal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The party against whom an order is made may bring an appeal to the Court of Appeal with the leave of the High Court or the Court of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similarly, clause 11 amends the existing section 74 such that a person against whom an order is made under that section may appeal against the order with the leave of the High Court or the Court of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These new powers were drawn from best practices in the United Kingdom (UK) and Canada.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In moving from a single touchpoint for vexatious proceedings under section 74 to a gradated approach, Courts are now better equipped to manage varying degrees of vexatious conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This accords with notions of fairness and also proportionality as litigants are restrained to different extents based on the severity of their vexatious conduct, instead of a one-size-fits-all approach under the current section 74.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, there are no automatic sanctions against the late filing of documents, and this tends to delay legal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These late filing fees seek to encourage parties and their lawyers to comply with the Rules of Court, Court orders and practice directions in relation to the filing of documents so that legal proceedings can be conducted and completed in a timely manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is an ongoing and worthy endeavour, for it has often been said, and in my view, correctly, that procedure is the handmaid of justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: By enhancing our Court processes, and strengthening Court procedures, while at the same time ensuring that the interests of litigants are safeguarded, these amendments will enable the Courts to continue to fulfil their mission of providing a just, efficient and effective avenue for all its users.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It helps to uphold the rule of law and plays an important part in the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Its importance and function in society do not diminish over time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But how it operates may need to adapt with the times.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, technology has been utilised by the Court to more efficiently and effectively manage cases.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill is important as it provides the necessary adaptations and tools to ensure that judicial resources are used judiciously in a manner that can best uphold rule of law and administration of justice in an effective and meaningful manner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In civil cases, property rights, livelihood and day-to-day provision may be at stake.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, pending Court proceedings and unsettled disputes are disruptive to the individuals and businesses involved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Timeliness of a just outcome is, therefore, imperative.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While a case is pending, landscapes of different industry sectors may change quickly, swiftly with commercial opportunities being lost or forgone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this juncture, Sir, allow me to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are three main areas of the Bill that I want to touch on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A common thread seems to be ensuring judicial resources are used judiciously while ensuring that parties’ substantive rights are protected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is with regard to vexatious litigants.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is to restrain a vexatious litigant from bringing spurious claims or applications that might clog the judicial process and hinder the effective administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While better calibration is a good objective, would there be more disputes over the fine distinctions each order in the regime requires?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the distinction between general and limited civil restraint order is that the general restraint order is limited to when the limited restraint order would not be sufficient or appropriate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another question I have is whether it was intended to set out a new and different test of “totally without merit”?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The original test of “without any reasonable ground” has been retained in section 74.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, would the Senior Minister of State elaborate on the difference between, if any, and the objectives of the two tests?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second area is development on the number of judges to constitute a coram under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is provided through clause 4 and the new Sixth Schedule in clause 18.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, a single judge is necessary for a consent judgment, a judgment which the parties have agreed on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As this list is being placed into a Schedule, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State what are some considerations that may be taken into account when this Schedule is amended, for example, what kind of trends, if any, will be considered and what factors will go into the decision regarding what level of judicial involvement, or what amount of judicial resources, are required?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The appeals process, according to Prof Pinsler in Principles of Civil Procedure, “ensures the integrity and correctness of judicial decision-making, preserves the certainty of the law through judicial precedent, develops jurisprudence and maintains public confidence in the administration of justice.” Therefore, the appellate function of the Court of Appeal is very important, and the amendments in this Bill must strengthen rather than reduce the Court of Appeal's ability to discharge its appellate function in an effective manner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires all new evidence regarding things that happened before the trial to pass the stringent special grounds test.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, the distinction between interlocutory appeals and judgments is removed and seems to restrict the judge’s discretion to admit additional evidence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, would the good Senior Minister of State explain the rationale behind such an amendment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to clause 6, the Court of Appeal may decide an appeal from the SICC without an oral hearing only upon the consent of every party.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State kindly elaborate on the rationale behind this?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, the Fourth and Fifth Schedules introduce more flexibility into what cases are non-appealable and appealable only with the leave of Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The press release states that this amendment is to “allow the list of matters specified in the Schedule to be amended quickly to adapt to demands on the ground.” Previously, the rationale as embedded and enunciated by the Court of Appeal in Open Net Pte Ltd vs the Info-communications Development Authority of Singapore is as follows: "The purpose underlying the Supreme Court of Judicature Act (SCJA) regarding the right to appeal is that an appeal to the Court of Appeal will generally be as of right for orders made at interlocutory applications which have the effect of finally disposing of the substantive rights of the parties; while an appeal to the Court of Appeal will ordinarily be denied for orders made at interlocutory applications which do not finally dispose of the substantive rights of the parties, and which are deemed to involve established principles of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe, on the whole, the Bill does that, and therefore, I support it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, I welcome the clarification that the Court may hear matters through live video or television link.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This aligns the legislative framework with the tools already at the disposal of Court users, such as the Technology Courts, and Mobile Technology Facility Services for use in non-technology Courtrooms and hearing chambers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While each amendment may be unremarkable on its own, the collective effect of all these amendments is to significantly encroach on the various aspects of the right to be heard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The right to be heard is a fundamental rule of natural justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be cautious when imposing any limits on that right.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I will be seeking clarifications on two matters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, the Minister's power to determine which civil matters may or may not be appealed to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the range of restraint orders that a Court may now grant for vexatious proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rationale for imposing these limits and the scope of their application should be clear so that litigants do not feel deprived of their right to be heard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Justice must both be done and be seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In its response to the public consultation conducted, the Ministry noted that there is sufficient accountability since the Minister is answerable to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rationale of moving the list of appealable and non-appealable civil matters from the main body of the text of the Act to the Schedule is to provide flexibility for amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this decision is a significant one that involves curtailing parties' rights of appeal, as was noted by respondents to the public consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Whether a civil matter should be appealable is a decision that warrants further deliberation and debate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendment suggests that the need for flexibility outweighs the value of deliberation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State elaborate further on why the list of appealable and non-appealable civil matters might need to be amended so urgently that it justifies moving the decision out of Parliament's oversight?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, sections 73A to 73D are significant new additions to the SCJA which grants the Court more tools to restrain unmeritorious and vexatious proceedings and litigants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new order that the Court may grant are intended to introduce a more nuanced approach to restrain a vexatious litigant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am concerned that the expanded powers may have the converse effect of leading to the Courts being more willing to resort to restraint orders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the factors that the Court should consider in determining whether a new action or application falls under an extended civil restraint order?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The wording of "involving, relating to, touching upon or leading to" in section 73C is taken from paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3 of the Practice Directions 3C of the UK’s Civil Procedure Rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the scope of the language under the new section 73C intended to be identical to the interpretation the UK courts have taken of extended civil restraint orders under their Civil Procedure Rules?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 73D(1) provides that the Court may make a general civil restraint order where an extended civil restraint order "would not be sufficient or appropriate".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State elaborate further on what factors the Court should consider in determining whether an extended civil restraint order is sufficient or appropriate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also provide some examples of when an extended civil restraint order would be deemed insufficient or inappropriate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, sections 73B(5), 73C(6) and 73D(6) allow a party subject to a restraint order to appeal where the High Court refuses to grant leave to commence an action or make an application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this right of appeal is in relation to the new application or action after a restraint order has already been made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the party have a right of appeal against the granting of the restraint order in the first place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the UK’s Civil Procedure Rules relating to civil restraint orders, an application for permission to commence an action or make an application may be determined without a hearing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify whether a hearing is necessary where a party applies for leave of Court to commence an action or make an application?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under sections 73C(5) and 73D(5), the Court may extend the period for which an extended or general civil restraint order remains in effect if it considers it appropriate to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify whether the Court has the power to do so on its own initiative or whether an application from a party is required?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the purpose behind the Bill, which is primarily to enhance the efficiency of the administration of justice whilst ensuring the litigants' legitimate interests are taken care of as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first is in relation to the application to adduce fresh evidence on appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed section 30 read with the 6th Schedule allows a Judge of Appeal sitting as the Court of Appeal to decide on an application to adduce fresh evidence in proceedings before the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, by way of a comparison, in relation to an application for extension of time to file a Notice of Appeal, a two-judge panel will hear the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed section 36(3) of the SCJA provides that a full Court of Appeal can discharge the order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the application to discharge or vary the order made by a Judge of Appeal can only be done with leave in the first place by the Judge of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the issue of whether or not to adduce fresh evidence can potentially have a bearing on the appeal, may I please ask what is the rationale of putting this issue before a one-judge Court of Appeal?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My concern is that we may have a situation where a Judge of Appeal, at first instance, refuses to give leave, and he then entrenches his decision by refusing to give leave for an application to discharge before a full Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, we would not have the possibility, however remote it may be, that a Judge of Appeal may get it wrong, and then there is no avenue to revisit his Honour's decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I ask about the policy of vesting amending powers with the Minister, as compared to the President.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members of this House will appreciate, our Government follows the Westminster model and the judiciary is a separate pillar of the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My respectful opinion is that the good thing about using the Minister is that the Minister is ultimately accountable to Parliament, and that I believe is a point that the hon Member Mr Louis Ng made earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, on the provisions allowing the Court of Appeal to decide via documents without the need for oral hearing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that section 34A(2) deals with appeals from the SICC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in relation specifically to the SICC, I note that it is provided that the documents-only appeal may be conducted when SICC issues an order for the same.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At first glance, in the absence of a consent order, it is rather strange for a division of the High Court to suggest to the Court of Appeal how it should conduct its proceedings in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I move on to the measures for dealing with unmeritorious or vexatious proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the proposed sections 73A to 73D are in addition to the existing section 74.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The learned Senior Minister of State mentioned about the limitation of the existing section 74.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He pointed out that section 74 may only be invoked through the application of the Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, however, note that the Attorney-General can also be an applying party under the provisions that will be introduced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This provision is not there in relation to the new section 73A to D.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, may I please ask why the same is not provided, given that the Attorney-General could be an applying party for either of these provisions?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The equality of arms issue is a real one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is not the case in relation to section 74(5) of SCJA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In practice, we sometimes see vexatious litigants commencing private prosecution which are criminal in nature.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The public prosecutor can intervene for each particular proceeding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But it may be useful to consider a situation where the powers contemplated under section 73A to D are extended to criminal proceedings, so that there could be a general restraint as the case may deserve.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will do my best to respond to them, also in the framework of the two broad baskets of revisions that have been introduced in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng, in particular, sought query on why that was being proposed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the amendments, as I said earlier, seek to consolidate all of these into one place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At present, you can find matters which are referred to, or necessary for leave to appeal, in the main body of the statute and also in the Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, likewise, for the matters which are non-appealable, also appearing in both places.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the first objective of these amendments is to put them all into one location, so that the Schedule itself, the Fourth and the Fifth, will house all the matters for which it is either non-appealable or appealable only with leave.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, moving them into the Schedules does allow for more flexibility and speed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the Members will know, it takes more time to amend the primary legislation than it will be to change the Schedules.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is not just the Minister alone who will decide on what goes in, what comes out, of the Schedules.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng did raise a concern as to whether the Schedules will remove the items going in or coming out from Parliament's oversight.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Minister, ultimately, is accountable in Parliament to all Members, and this would apply to the decisions as regards what goes in or comes out of the Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To the extent that there are any issues to be raised on this, Parliament can be the forum for this to be raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On a related note, Mr Christopher de Souza did question as to whether there is a change in the policy rationale as to how a matter or the basis on which a matter is classified as non-appealable or appealable only with leave, within the SCJA framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Matters are and will continue to be carefully differentiated based on their importance to the substantive outcome and also, quite importantly, balanced against the appropriate allocation of judicial resources to deal with those matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai queried why the power to amend the Schedules is vested in the Minister, but the power to amend the monetary limit under section 34(2)(a) is not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to that extent, that remains the province of the President and it finds its place in the main body of the statute, whereas the cases which go into the Schedules can be decided upon by the Minister in consultation with the Chief Justice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to clause 4 of the Bill which introduces the new Schedule, the Sixth Schedule, which sets out the coram of the Court of Appeal when exercising civil jurisdiction in matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked what considerations may be taken into account when deciding on the Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The key considerations would be the appropriate amount of judicial resources which should be expended on a particular class of matter, obviously issues as to the complexity and the novelty of the matters raised will remain high on the list of priority.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, as Mr de Souza knows, the Courts already consider complexity and novelty in deciding when to constitute a coram of three or five judges in a Court of Appeal as the case may be, for both civil and criminal appeals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For instance, a coram consisting of three Judges of Appeal would generally not be necessary to deal with matters incidental to determining the merits of the application or the primary application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, applications which have bearing on seeking security for costs or applying to discharge solicitors, those do not need the full coram of three.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to deal with the question of further evidence in proceedings and I think all three Members touched on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, in particular, asked about the rationale as to why leave will now be required to admit further evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, bear that in mind as you understand the concept and the construct on why these rules apply in this way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Most parties, I think Members would agree, would have the opportunity of raising all the evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have our hearings now conducted first with extensive exchange of cases in writing and then the submissions by the skeletals as well just before the hearing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, several written opportunities would be afforded to the parties already before the hearing itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is in contradistinction to those cases where, subsequent to the hearing itself, new matters develop and, in those situations, I think it is reasonable to assume that if they have a bearing on the outcome of the appeal, satisfying the usual test for admission of evidence, then the evidence would be allowed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would stress that this process strikes a proper balance between the right of the parties to rely on and adduce further evidence, and also the appropriate use of judicial and Court time in dealing with these matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, I turn to dealing with matters that can be disposed of based on written submissions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Murali Pillai touched on this question, and asked questions as to why section 34A(2), which allows the Court of Appeal to decide matters based on written submissions, is only restricted to appeals from SICC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai further pointed out that section 34A(1) already provides that the Court of Appeal has the power to decide on matters without hearing oral arguments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The scope of this provision applies to potential applications which are ancillary to the main appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, as I said in my opening speech earlier, they deal with applications, not the main substantive appeal itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An example of such an "application" would be, going back to my earlier point, security for costs or applying to amend a part of the case, or trying to deal with the potential cost of the hearing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, those are matters that are ancillary to, but not the main appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a general principle nonetheless, where oral arguments are otherwise useful to elucidate the issues and to facilitate a just and expeditious disposal of an appeal before the Court of Appeal, those will still take place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, Mr Murali Pillai raised the question of SICC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SICC is set up to hear international and commercial matters which involve parties with no substantial connection to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Given that such matters may involve international parties or foreign registered lawyers, the parties may wish, on their own accord, to save time by obviating the need for the oral hearing to take place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, any international judges on the coram would also not be required to travel to Singapore for that oral hearing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such a flexibility makes SICC a more attractive option for international parties to settle their disputes and also adds to the already existing suite of party-centric innovations, such as allowing foreign counsel to submit directly on foreign law without it having to be proven through expert evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the choice is made by the parties themselves, and not, as I think Mr Murali Pillai suggested, by the SICC, which yes, remains as a division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to the next basket of amendments which deal with controlling vexatious conduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would preface my response by reminding Members that the power to control vexatious conduct is already present.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 10 of the Bill introduces the new civil restraint orders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are meant, in the first instance, to be used in situations where the litigants have persistently initiated proceedings that are groundless and without merit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the litigant has to do it more than once, multiple times, at least twice in the case of the first rung or the lowest grade of the orders, and also without merit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are done often with the purpose of annoying or embarrassing the other party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I wish to inform Members that the litigants who are held to be "vexatious litigants" by our Courts have so far been far and few, thankfully.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The policy intention behind these amendments is, as I mentioned earlier, to allow the Courts to have, and to be able to take, a more nuanced approach in terms of the orders that they make in managing the different levels of culpability of the vexatious litigants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this allows the judges to have more regard to the individual circumstances of each case and to make those distinctions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, in terms of how and when these orders are to be applied, it will be for the Courts to carefully consider all the facts and circumstances of each case before exercising their discretion on whether to do so or not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While I will clarify the ambit of each of these restraint orders shortly, the jurisprudence in this area must ultimately be left to be developed through the exercise of principled discretion by our judges, based on the actual facts and the context before them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members would wish to note that this is also the position in the UK.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With these in mind, let me address the concerns raised by Members, which, as I have heard, broadly falls into three categories.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the definition and applicability of each of the civil restraint orders; second, the procedural details subsequent to the grant of a civil restraint order; and third, the interaction and, as Mr Murali Pillai puts it, the interplay between the civil restraint orders and section 74 of SCJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, I wish to emphasise that each of the three types of civil restraint orders requires a distinct threshold to be met before they can be considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While some cases may inevitably throw out a factual matrix where the type of order to issue is not so clear-cut and not so cut and dry, I would say that the Courts would be well-placed to apply the letter and intent of the law to these new and potentially multifarious situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And they would do so having regard to the issue at hand, to the party in question and to the conduct in question as well in each individual case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may be helpful to consider that these restraint orders have, in fact, been applied in jurisdictions like the UK, like I mentioned, and as far as we can tell, they have not faced issues with regard to the way in which one might distinguish the type of orders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The factors I believe are clear, and they have been considered in previous cases also in the UK.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And our Courts will no doubt take reference too, although it will not be strictly bound by these cases, when they have regard to these applications with the specific facts before them in question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked what factors the Court would consider when deciding whether an extended civil restraint order is sufficient or appropriate, given that a general civil restraint order will be issued if an extended civil restraint order would not be sufficient or appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To answer Mr Louis Ng's query, one scenario in which the general civil restraint order would be imposed would be where, for example, a vexatious litigant adopts a "blunderbuss approach" to litigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He may bring in a slew of grievances against different parties, within a short period of time, without focusing on a particular single grievance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The language that I have just quoted is from a UK decision applying their equivalent of the statute.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, I believe, gives the Court an ability to appreciate, in a particular case, the number of cases that are filed, the number of times the Court has faced with applications by this litigant, the period of time within which it is done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for instance if you file five cases over 10 years, it is quite different from five cases over two months.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the Court is able to appreciate that better in the context of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court would also look at whether it is widespread, whether it is indiscriminate and whether one raises a series of allegations which have, basically, no legal merit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another example is if the litigant just takes an approach that seeks to sully the name of a potential party with no reasonable legal basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all that comes into play and comes into the mix.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the flexibility of this approach allows the Court to attenuate its response based on the facts of the instant case before it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, I would like to touch on the scope of the extended civil restraint orders under the new section 73C, a point that Mr Louis Ng raised, the question of the scope of the language under the new section 73C and whether it is intended to be identical to the interpretation the UK courts have taken under their Civil Procedure Rules, and the factors that the Court should consider in determining whether a new action or application falls under the extended civil restraint order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When construing the new section 73C, the position adopted by the UK courts may be persuasive, but our Courts are obviously not bound to follow their interpretation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Different considerations in different jurisdictions will obviously dictate differences in the approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if the Courts can extend the period for which an extended or general civil restraint order remains in effect on its own motion or if an application from a party is required.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On whether such extension is appropriate, the UK courts have considered whether there is sufficient evidence to demonstrate that there was reasonable apprehension of future vexatious conduct following the expiry of the original extended or general civil restraint order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And there is an authority on this if Members are interested, that is, Ashcroft vs Webster, which is a 2017 decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, one of the factors which the court will look at and have regard to in the UK would be the conduct of the party against whom the orders were made, subsequent to the making of the order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether a party will have a right of appeal against the grant of a civil restraint order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where appropriate, the Court of Appeal, as you heard earlier, would be entitled to hear this also on paper.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But it takes into account the gravity of the issue, the nuances in terms of the complexity and the novelty of the matter and then decide whether it will be assisted by oral hearing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these factors would come in to bear.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I now move on to Mr Murali Pillai's questions on the interplay between the civil restraint orders and section 74, and whether there remains a useful role for section 74.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Furthermore, unlike the new civil restraint orders, section 74 is not limited to civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it also applies to criminal proceedings which the provisions in the SCJA Bill do not do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about the reason for not extending the application of the new civil restraint orders to criminal proceedings, in particular, private prosecutions instituted by vexatious litigants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Notably, civil restraint orders are adopted from the UK, which only applies these orders to civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If, however, circumstances change, and there is a proliferation of similar issues in the criminal proceedings space, then that matter can be revisited.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As for the issue of private prosecutions raised by Mr Murali Pillai, the control of these proceedings, ultimately, lies with the Public Prosecutor as well and the Public Prosecutor can intervene at any stage of the proceedings, as Mr Murali Pillai correctly pointed out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to that extent, the power remains vested with the Public Prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if it is vexatious and if there is otherwise any issue which causes concern to the Public Prosecutor, then those powers under section 13 of the CPC can be exercised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The concern, therefore, about any potential abuse by vexatious litigants who initiate private prosecutions can be adequately addressed by or within the existing criminal procedure framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also raised several other questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, in relation to the assignment of advocate and solicitor, and he asked why the new provisions relating to the civil restraint orders do not provide that the High Court shall assign an advocate and solicitor to the party against whom such an order is sought, unlike section 74.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I said, section 74 now remains in its place to deal with the most severe of cases which attract the most severe of restrictions and it also deals with criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A general civil restraint order can be extended, but only for a maximum period of two years at any given occasion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, as I mentioned earlier, section 74 continues to apply to criminal proceedings and an order under section 74 has more severe consequences in such a scenario as it can potentially affect a person's life and liberty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, having regard to all these factors, it is more appropriate to ensure that legal representation is mandated in such cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why section 74 provides for that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nonetheless, legal aid and the other pro bono assistance will continue, subject to the usual requirements; they will remain available for all parties who require but are not able to afford legal representation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to Mr Christopher de Souza's observation that the test under the civil restraint orders is "totally without merit" while the test under section 74 is "without any reasonable ground".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think Mr de Souza sought elaboration on the differences between the two tests and the objectives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I note that it is also the case in the UK that the "totally without merit" phrase or requirement is used for civil restraint orders, whilst the "without any reasonable ground" requirement is used for the equivalent provision to our section 74.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we borrowed from that provision and we retained this distinction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This does not appear to have caused the UK courts any difficulty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But obviously, we will continue to watch this space as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The modifications to Court procedures will improve the Courts' management of their caseload, which will go some way towards ensuring that parties resolve their disputes expeditiously, and that is also in line with enhancing the interests of justice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By arming the Courts with a suite of measures to respond to litigants who, having had their day in Court, abuse the right to be heard by pursuing vexatious proceedings, the Courts will be able to husband their finite resources better and channel them to where they are most needed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is no doubt that the improvement of Court procedures is and remains work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As time goes by, we can expect to see further developments, such as in information technology and the like, which disrupt the way things are done today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Going forward, we will review the impact of the present amendments, continue to work with Members to consider if further improvements ought to be made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, in doing so, we will also study the best practices of similar jurisdictions overseas to ascertain what best practices can be and should be imported into Singapore.
